candidate.blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential: identify transfusion compatibility risks, verify blood products, and prevent adverse transfusion events through correct interpretation of blood-group information.
candidate.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — emergency ABO red-cell compatibility
candidate.educational_objective: Recognize group O red cells as the ABO-compatible emergency red-cell choice when recipient ABO type is not yet known, while distinguishing red-cell compatibility from plasma compatibility and avoiding overgeneralization to Rh selection.

options.A: Group O red blood cells lack A and B antigens and can be used for recipients of other ABO groups when emergency red-cell transfusion is required before typing is known.
options.B: Group O red blood cells are universal recipients and can receive red cells from every ABO group.
options.C: Group O red blood cells express both A and B antigens, which makes them compatible with all recipients.
options.D: AB plasma and group O red cells use the same ABO compatibility rule because plasma and red-cell compatibility are interchangeable.

candidate.rationale: AABB states that in an emergency anyone can receive type O red blood cells, which is why people with type O blood are commonly described as universal red-cell donors. This ABO red-cell compatibility principle is different from plasma compatibility; AABB separately notes that individuals of all ABO types can receive AB plasma. Therefore A is correct. B reverses donor/recipient terminology, C incorrectly states that group O red cells express A and B antigens, and D incorrectly treats red-cell and plasma compatibility as interchangeable. Rh selection and other compatibility considerations are outside the deliberately limited ABO-red-cell scope of this item.
candidate.source_claim_supported: For ABO red-cell compatibility, group O red cells can be used in emergencies before a recipient's ABO type is known; this does not mean group O is a universal recipient or that plasma compatibility follows the same rule.
candidate.source_document_title: FAQs About Blood and Blood Donation
candidate.source_locator: About Blood > Most common blood type: in an emergency, anyone can receive type O red blood cells; people with type O blood are known as universal donors. The same section states that individuals of all types can receive type AB plasma, demonstrating component-specific ABO compatibility.
candidate.source_organization: Association for the Advancement of Blood & Biotherapies (AABB)
candidate.stem: During an emergency red-cell transfusion before the recipient's ABO type is known, why may group O red blood cells be selected?
